extracted.intended_audience: literary critics and readers evaluating prose style
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the quality and authorship of prose (autobiography, religious/inspirational writing) with emphasis on clarity, diction, consistency, originality, and fitness of rhetorical devices. Uses examples and anti-patterns to illustrate good vs bad practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good English (clean, compact, dignified, workman-like)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose should be 'clean, compact, dignified, almost perfect'—not necessarily immaculate, but generally polished and competent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training and persistent practice improve prose to this state. Twain contrasts the 'good' English of Science and Health with the clumsy miscellaneous writings to show how a text can reach a professional standard through revision and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkwardness of expression / ambiguous phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences must not be constructed so that their meaning is unclear or open to multiple unintended interpretations (e.g., uncertainty about who a casualty happened to).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test sentences for legal-like ambiguity: if sent to a court, would the meaning be provable? Reword or supply clearer referents (e.g., move relative pronouns) to remove ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun-reference clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns (we, who, it, etc.) should have obvious and correct antecedents; avoid stray or misplaced 'who' that confuses meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Many pale cripples went into the Church leaning on crutches who came out carrying them on their shoulders'—reposition 'who' to follow 'cripples' to clarify who is being described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential, orderly narrative movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative should move in an orderly, sequential fashion rather than rambling, skipping around, or wandering without purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rambling that lacks discernible artistic intention marks an 'apprentice' hand; experienced writers may skip or fragment for effect, but it should be purposeful and advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of style across works and registers
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should sustain a comparable level of diction and competence across different types of writing (e.g., private autobiography vs. doctrinal treatise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked discrepancies (one work nearly perfect, another juvenile and affected) suggest differing authorship, heavy editorial intervention, or uneven craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation, artificiality, and pretentiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose should not display showy, sophomoric, or self-indulgent ornament—'affectation, artificiality; their makeup is a complacent and pretentious outpour of false figures and fine writing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for gratuitous foreignisms, ostentatious allusions, and 'pet poetic picturesquenesses' that serve self-display rather than meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors responsibly (no 'metaphor gone insane')
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors must fit and illuminate, not multiply into confused, insane or incoherent imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing incongruous images or inventing figures that obscure rather than clarify; when metaphor proliferates uncontrolled, it becomes an anti-pattern (e.g., 'Intoxicated Metaphor').

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful vocabulary; don't employ large words gratuitously
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using big or learned words merely because they are pretty or showy; diction should serve clarity and appropriateness, not ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of misused or unnecessary grand words (noumenon, foresplendor, foreto'gallant) illustrate how learned-sounding language can be misplaced, especially in autobiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate register for the genre (plainness in autobiography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a diction and tone suited to the genre; autobiography favors straightforward, unadorned expression rather than lofty, sermon-like phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grandiose theological metaphors and rhetorical flourishes feel out of place in personal narrative and undermine trust in the voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and coherence (avoid irrelevant interjections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t insert ostentatious or irrelevant clauses (e.g., sudden 'God is over us all') that break coherence and fail to advance the thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such devices may momentarily dazzle but leave the reader puzzled; discourse should progress logically without gratuitous digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise grammatical usage and idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correct idiom and grammar (e.g., battles are 'waged', not 'wage'); errors of usage mark carelessness or lack of craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small but telling grammatical mistakes reveal a writer's limits and should be caught by careful revision or copyediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and headings should match content
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter headings and section titles must accurately represent the content they introduce (e.g., 'Marriage and Parentage' misleading when it concerns motherhood only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose headings that avoid reader deception and clarify structure; mismatched headings create confusion and weaken credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous proofreading and editorial oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreading should catch awkward constructions, misplaced words, grammatical slips, and printer's errors; failure suggests insufficient editorial control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain suggests a proofreader should be 'shot' for allowing basic errors; in practice, employ attentive editors and multiple passes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition and meaningless amplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not stack redundancies or illogical phrases (e.g., 'increase be added to perfection'); avoid tautology and puffery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tighten sentences to remove needless amplifiers that add no semantic content and only bloat prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and freshness of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose should show originality rather than 'destitution of originality' and repetition of 'pet' images and formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on the same stock metaphors and repeated poetic pictures signals creative poverty; seek new, appropriate expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentatious scholarly allusions used as stage-properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Dropping Greek, Hebrew, or Latin references for effect rather than substance is an affectation—'affectations of scholarly learning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusions must be relevant and comprehensible to the audience; otherwise they read as self-aggrandizement and weaken rhetorical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of voice / person (avoid erratic shifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistent narrative person (I/we/third person); erratic shifts or unverifiable collective pronouns ('we' for 'I') confuse authorship and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts such as using 'we' intermittently then reverting to third person signal instability of voice and reduce reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful use of scriptural or authoritative quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations (scripture, etc.) should be used to illuminate or argue, not merely to make a loud ornament or substitute for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'fire off a Scripture-verse where it will make the handsomest noise'; ensure quoted material connects to and advances the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstantial evidence in authorship attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate claims of authorship by stylistic/circumstantial evidence: consistent stylistic fingerprints, recurrent errors, and disparity between texts can indicate differing authorship or heavy editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain uses differences in diction, recurring flaws, and distribution of polished vs. crude passages as grounds to doubt single authorship; apply systematic stylistic comparison when attributing texts.
